As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.
One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.
Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.
Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?
Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

• A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's former congressional seat and is already pushing for federal action — warning that "we could sleepwalk into a disaster."
• Recursive self-improvement is keeping him up at night: A recent report suggesting Anthropic may have achieved AI that meaningfully advances itself rattled Wiener, who sees it as proof that Congress is running out of time to act before losing control entirely.
• He wants regulation with real teeth: Wiener is pushing for a powerful federal AI regulator, whistleblower protections, kill switches, and auditing requirements — and he's firmly against federal laws that would strip states of their own ability to regulate.
• Cautious optimism, with caveats: Wiener is concerned about Congress's poor track record on tech regulation, wary of Trump's hostility to AI safety concerns, and hoping any crisis that forces action will be, as he puts it, "as small as possible."

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.
I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.
“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”
Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”
Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.
Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.
“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”
Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.
He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.
And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”
Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”
He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

items.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry

items.content:
As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.
Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”
Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.
“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.
These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.
Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

AI正在毁掉我的计算机学位。
写下这行控诉的，是一个从小梦想学计算机的大二女生，Katie。
没有名校光环，高中数学只拿了个B；此前也没接受过任何科班集训，唯一拿得出手的「项目经历」，不过是几个略显简陋的网页小游戏。
原本以为，迈进大学象牙塔，终于能好好学计算机了！
谁曾想——
课程大纲是Claude批量生成的，期末大作业是LLM自动批改的，就连导师发来的关怀邮件，很可能也是后台自动化脚本。。。
面对这荒诞的一幕，她瘫软了（bushi）：
由于AI，我的大学似乎正在经历一场生死存亡的危机。
博客发布不到24小时，光速成Hacker News首页热榜第一。
彻底崩坏的计算机系
在她的求学经历里，自打这波生成式AI爆发后，学校的教学政策就没停止过反复横跳。
最开始当然是全面拥抱：
给学生作业打分写评语、生成课程大纲、发全员催学邮件……全给安排上了大模型。
结果呢？
折腾不到三个月，发现全是幻觉与垃圾内容，光速撤回。
整套教学管理，始终处于一种极其精神分裂的状态——
你们绝对不能使用AI！
哦不，说错了，所有人必须使用AI！
不对不对……好像还是不能用AI啊……
然后就会出现一个很魔幻的事。
同一门课程，上一个模块的作业，教授强制要求你用AI，说这是这门课成绩的重要考核维度。
听罢，你咬咬牙，自掏腰包开通了Claude订阅。
到了下一个模块，你满怀自信地上传了站起来蹬Opus 5.5调教出来的代码，结果——
不er?
什么叫学术不端，使用LLM要扣分？？？
但说实话，如果只是规则朝令夕改，也还好，可以勉强应付。
最让作者破防的是，自己努力学习考上大学，付这么高的学费，就是指望能跟着专家教授系统学习。
结果，你个大学教授也拿Claude糊弄我？？？
是的，讲台上的导师一边严厉警告学生不要投机取巧，转过头自己直接把需求丢给Claude，一键生成教学资料。
以前的作业，好歹是教授结合教学目标深思熟虑、在教研组过过一遍的。任务体量适中，循序渐进。
现在？妹子怀疑这帮教授连MD都没打开过。
满篇都是大模型生成的废话。3000字作业说明，要提交15份材料。
掐指一算，作业量比以前翻了三倍……
结果就是，那些本来数学底子就薄、转专业跨考过来的普通学生，只能被逼着去走马观花地速通知识点。
我来这里是为了踏踏实实学真东西的，该死的，不是为了在一份3000字的作业里对着15个根本完不成的任务浮于表面！
但这还不是最崩溃的。
很多同学辛辛苦苦研究了十几天，但不知道为啥，就是怎么也跑不通。
结果在DDL前一周，老师突然发了一封勘误邮件：
大纲里有两个地方写错了，现已修正，请大家重新提交。
你还我白烧的这么多Token😭
所以，到底为什么要这么干？
Katie表示，倒也不能全怪教授们。罪魁祸首还是管理层。
你知道资方最喜欢听什么吗？规模化学习，最好是自动化的！
这样，他们就可以在不支付额外员工费用的情况下，尽可能多地从学费中榨取利润。
既然大模型能自动化出题，能秒批作业，那为什么还要花大价钱去聘请助教、增加讲师编制？
技术成了校方无限度削减教学支出的借口，无止境地压榨讲师，工作量多到光靠人的注意力根本完成。
Katie也提到，自己平时根本见不着导师的影子。
唯一的联系是，她在好几天没登录线上学习平台时，会收到一封导师的来信——
结果满怀紧张地打开一看，原来不是导师本人写的，这玩意儿是触发的自动警报o(╥﹏╥)o。
Hacker News最热门
帖子发布后，很快火爆全网，迅速登上Hacker News首页榜一。
评论区也涌入了很多计算机老哥。
但出乎我意料的是，就算同为计算机系，竟然也并不都是共情的声音。
整个计算机技术社区，割裂成了两极。
一派是早已在行业立足的资深老鸟。
在他们的视角下，当下的种种混乱，不过是技术范式演进过程中的短暂阵痛。
我已经从事这一职业超过二十年了，每天都能学到新的东西。在过去几年里，随着人工智能技术的发展，我的学习速度更快了，也能更深入地了解我所工作的系统。
总而言之就是，AI终归只是一件趁手的工具。只要善用大模型进行苏格拉底式的循循诱导，当下的学习资源，不知比他们那时候强出多少倍。
人工智能并不会取代教育和传统的学习方式。
相反，人工智能会提升你理解和记忆的能力。对于一个技术思维较强且自学的专业人士来说，我一直渴望的是持续学习下去。
因此，不少经验丰富的前辈对新一代新人反而带着几分艳羡：
成为一名高级工程师，并不真的取决于你从事软件开发的时间长短。我见过一些非常出色的21岁开发者，他们的编程能力甚至能超越那些已经工作20多年的人。
我认为，他们能能表现如此出色的原因，在于他们具备扎实的计算机科学基础知识。
但这终究是属于少数人的叙事。
另一端，绝大多数刚毕业的年轻人，只感到了窒息。
有跟帖者贴出了一项量化研究结论：
斯坦福大学的研究人员发现，他们去年所预测的初级职员的就业趋势仍然持续存在且正在扩大。
具体来说，那些从事最易受人工智能影响行业的22至25岁员工的就业水平，比那些不常面临人工智能冲击的同行低19%。
对此，一些常年参与招聘的从业者也坦率印证了这一现实：
确实，与其花时间培养一个从零起步的应届生，不如给资深工程师配上顶配的Coding Agent来得高效。
我真的不知道应该给即将毕业的开发者什么建议。
花费四年青春学计算机，最后连工作都找不到……
那，CS学位的意义，究竟是什么？
找回编程的温度
对于这个问题，我觉得，或许能在Katie那篇博客，找到答案。
文章最后，她写下了这么一段文字：
我才不管计算机科学和数学是不是已经走到头了！我还是想学！
好吧，我确实关心自己未来的职业发展，但这也不意味着我想忘掉已经学过的一切，或者停下探索的脚步。
还有那么多有趣的方向值得探索，有些和AI有关，有些没有。可铺天盖地的标题总在说什么「软件工程完了」「不用AI就会被淘汰」之类的，让人喘不过气。
难道女孩就不能单纯为了好玩学学统计学吗？
经历了这一切后，Katie给出的答案是——
我可以继续，但我不会了。这会让我消化不良。
也许我会回到OpenProcessing上，做一些更愚蠢的游戏。
至少，现在我真的知道如何做一些编程了。
然后，她贴出了自己早年间在OpenProcessing上写的几个简陋小网页：
一个放着带感音乐的简单太空射击游戏；
一只点一下就会「喵」一声的莫古利；
还有一个用麦克风声音把小鱼吓跑的互动demo。
实话说，非常粗糙。
任何一个拎出来，都比如今Astra、Fable一句Prompt直出的效果差了十万八千里。
甚至可能还不如一个新模型的鹈鹕自行车demo有热度。。。
但点开的一瞬间，你就是能感受到一种，模型永远无法生成的东西——
生命力。
那是很多程序员最初爱上写代码时的模样。
不是为了在求职流水线上刷穿几百道LeetCode，不是为了在周报里汇报又省了多少Token的调用账单，更不是为了迎合大厂中层拍脑袋想出来的效能指标。
在这一切被功利化规训之前，原本仅仅是在黑底白字的终端里敲下几行字符，看着屏幕上亮起的像素点按照自己的心意运转流动，就足以让人兴奋得通宵难眠。
我们亲手造就了近乎无所不知的超级机器。
但却似乎在不知不觉中，把人类最原始的探索欲与沉浸感，关在了门外……

混元Hy4正式交卷了！
腾讯这次上来根本不跟你客气，态度就明晃晃写在脸上：跻身最强开源模型之列。
770B总参数、49B激活参数，首次引入原生视觉能力、首次支持电脑操作。
指令遵循、长文理解和长程Agent能力也一起升级，电脑操作、长程Agent任务都挤进了开源阵营前排。
从preview到正式版，Hy4显著扩展了预训练和后训练的数据与训练规模，甚至还直接跑去跟一线业务搞起了“Co-Design”联合打磨。
WorkBuddy国内版、国际版已经同步完成首发接入！
我就先在WorkBuddy里给它出了个难题：给我搓一把完全可交互的3D机械键盘出来。
75%配列、84键，键帽、轴体、定位板、PCB、电池和外壳，六层结构都安排上了。
鼠标拽着能原地炸开看内部做工，装回去还能直接上手敲，连按键下压、弹簧受力回弹的物理动效都给你算进去了。
这么一看，制作新品展示demo的活儿不就有人干了？你说是吧Hy4～
Hy4已经在腾讯云TokenHub、WorkBuddy/CodeBuddy、元宝、企业微信智能助理大圆、ima等产品上线；API同步接入OpenRouter、Hermes、OpenCode等平台。
QQ、王者荣耀、和平精英、微信读书、腾讯新闻等腾讯系产品也在持续接入中。
模型权重也将于近期开源。
那咱也话不多说，先来实测一波。
像素级视觉感知
Hy4首次引入的视觉理解，细节识别已经精细到能够在28亿像素航拍图中，定位约2米的屋顶构件。
这眼神儿是真不错。
那咱接下来也考考它的眼力。
第一道题，照着一张设计截图，做一个复古风格的音乐播放器。
先不说高清航拍图，我就想看看，它到底能不能看懂排版细节。
Hy4接单之后先把图里的配色、字体、布局挨个拆了一遍，连左侧栏宽多少像素都量好了，然后才开始写代码，把页面和播放功能一起搭起来。
中间裁切工具出了点偏差，它还换了个办法，直接分析像素来定位线条、提取颜色。
行，做题还自带尺子和色卡。
看到成品的那一刻，我盯着屏幕看了足足半分钟，不er，这还原度得99.9%吧——
米色打底、橙红点缀、黄绿配色，再加上粗粗的大标题和一张黑胶唱片，复古味儿一下就上来了。
导航、歌单、播放区域和待播列表，也都待在该待的位置。
我把买家秀和卖家秀并排放着找了半天不同，最显眼的居然是左上角那俩前进后退按钮：一个圆，一个方。。。
属于是不拿放大镜看，都不知道该从哪儿挑刺。
翻了翻Hy4的交付说明，播放暂停、上下首切换、拖动进度、调节音量都接上了，循环、随机播放、搜索和收藏同步也没落下。
连手懒得碰鼠标的情况都考虑到了：空格控制播放，方向键调整进度。
然而当我点下播放键才发现，它连三首测试曲子都给备好了。
我没给它传任何音频文件啊！
视频地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ
原来这些曲子是它用浏览器原生的Web Audio实时合成的，不用我再满电脑翻音频文件，打开网页就能听。
好好好，我只给了一张图，Hy4不仅交付了播放器，还附赠测试曲库，顺手把试音的活儿也包了。
接着翻它的自测流水。
照记录里的过程，Hy4写完代码后，自己悄悄在后台拉起了一个无头Chrome浏览器，在沙盒环境里对着各个UI按钮挨个点击、拖拽，一边点一边截图做视觉差异对比。
第一轮其实也没一把全过：
51项过了48项，两项卡在测试脚本，最后一项被它自己揪出来——列表放完最后一首歌，再点下一首时逻辑没处理闭环。
它反手把这个边缘Case改了，重新跑回归。
最终报告显示，59项测试全部通过，控制台报错和运行时异常均为零。
光二维界面还不够过瘾，我又扔给Hy4一张游乐场平面图，让它把园子给“立”起来。
设施在哪儿、多大，路怎么拐弯，都得照着图来；摩天轮和旋转木马也不能光站着摆造型，得转起来；这游乐园还得能让我进去逛。
经历了一连串几何体建模、着色器配置和摄像机绑定，它真的把整座“星光游乐园”原地拔地而起了。
经典的红白旋转木马顶棚、主路两旁的小卖部、沿街分布的低多边形树木与草皮，全按比例投射进了三维空间。
低多边形画风也挺清爽，看着像个适合摸鱼时进去溜达两圈的小游戏。
我本来都做好了进门先迷路的准备，右上角居然还配了张小地图：设施、道路、草坪，连我现在站哪儿都标出来了。
进园后，WASD移动，鼠标拖动转向，按住Shift还能加速，想看设施就打开标签。
逛晕了还能一键返回入口，主打一个随时找得着北。
它甚至准备了“沿道路自动巡游”的按钮，点一下，连路都不用自己走。
好嘛，让它建个游乐园，导览服务也一起开张了。
视频地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ
Agent交付力拉满
游乐园逛完，回来干点正事，试试Hy4这次重点强化的Agent和长程任务能力。
我给它塞了一份“拾光Beam Go 2”便携智能投影仪的产品资料，让它做套15页左右的新品介绍PPT。
Hy4先把资料从头捋了一遍，配图也没瞎找，直接利用原生代码绘制风格高度统一的矢量示意图，图表则保留成可编辑的形式，方便后续修改。
在渲染第4页时，它发现一段长文本挤出了页面安全边框，自己在后台立刻重构版式，把单栏拆成了卡片流，二次校验通过后才继续往下推进。
最后一共交了16页PPT。行，还多送一页。
不过，打工人都懂，PPT做完了，往往才是改PPT的开始。
我又扔给它一份完全不同视觉体系的暗黑高对比度模板，要求它按新版式重刷一遍。
Hy4倒没急着把16页全改了，先挑一页试着套进去，确认没问题，再批量修改剩下的页面。
不得不说，边验证边工作的能力是它这次非常亮眼的优势，不是一股脑输出完就交差，而是小步试错、验证通过再推进，大幅减少返工。
接着，我又给Hy4派了个活儿：
做一个高可用性的图片批量处理工具。
裁切、改尺寸、压缩、导出，单张图折腾几下还行，一批图挨个来，鼠标没坏，人先麻了。
这次干脆把重复的手工操作交给它。
Hy4领到任务后，先在环境里去研读了业内开源标杆Squoosh和Image Workspace的优秀设计，借鉴了原图/压缩图对比滑杆、预设工作流的技术方案。
然后快速拆分出上传流、处理流、Web Worker多线程并行、Canvas图形管线、ZIP归档模块，直接敲代码。
成品交付的时候，名字都起好了——
ATELIER影像批处理工作台。
米白底色、橙色点缀，打开先弹出三步引导。Slogan是：“把重复的交给工具，把审美留给自己。”
行，我负责审美，它负责重复。
按交付设计，图片可以整批拖入，也能直接选文件夹；左侧统一设置裁切、尺寸、压缩和格式，少数需要“特殊照顾”的图片，再单独调整。
它还顺手内置了社交头像1:1、电商主图、极小体积等常用配方，拉动滑杆能实时看画质损失，最后点击一次打包成ZIP扔给浏览器下载。
视频地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ
除此之外，Hy4现在还真能拿起鼠标干活。
打开Chrome里的JS Paint，用鼠标临摹混元亲亲表情包，还得把操作过程录下来。
视频地址？：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/OThj_29CAuHn6ioaqjkSpQ
看屏幕、找工具、选颜色，再控制鼠标落笔，用上的正是它新支持的CUA（计算机使用）能力。
好嘛，别的AI忙着一键出图，Hy4在这儿练鼠绘，上有参考图负责考眼力，下有画图软件负责考手艺（doge）。
加量不加价
实测玩这么一圈，我最大的感受是，Hy4在长程任务中的自主执行完成度高了很多。
面对多步骤任务，它能够持续保持目标与任务状态，在执行过程中进行阶段性自检，根据运行结果定位问题、修改方案，再重新验证，直到能交付无Bug的结果。
我前面的案例确实也都是它自主执行、检查和修改后的一次性交付结果。
Hy4的这轮训练也更追求在真实生产力场景发挥作用。
前端优化细化到了复杂交互、业务逻辑、状态管理及前后端联动；
对Blender、CAD等专业软件和跨应用长程任务也进行了专项训练，强化任务规划与执行能力。
办公场景下，Hy4还围绕时效检索、多源信息整合和事实一致性校验，对搜索链路进行了专项优化。
在内部测试中，Hy4的幻觉率由preview版的12.95%降至7.2%，推测类错误率由23.1%降至5.6%；
金融这边，Hy4还专门补了一轮专业课。
训练覆盖基金研究、证券分析、量化策略、资产配置、公司金融和财税会计等方向，基于真实场景构建了数千个工作空间、上万个高质量任务，让模型学习专业流程与规范。
共有213位专家参与众测，其中七成来自外部头部金融机构，拥有五年以上工作经验——
这批阅卷人，可没那么好糊弄。
结果579个真实金融任务测下来，Hy4综合表现位居开源模型第一。
看来这轮“进修”，还真没白上。
科研任务的跨度也正在扩大。
Hy4将复杂推理、科学编程与长程执行结合，在涵盖7大学科、123项可执行研究任务的TenureTrail内部评测中，展现了数学构造、物理建模等领域的科研能力。
面对包含699万个单细胞、整整84张没有任何时间空间连续标记的二维无序小鼠胚胎切片的数据集还混杂着实验切片中常见的镜像翻转等噪声数据；在离线运行、无专用配准工具、无细胞类型标注的严苛条件下，Hy4耗时1.5小时，自主完成小鼠胚胎切片的空间对齐与三维网格重构。
全程零人工干预，最终对齐精细度甚至干掉了专业配准工具的默认配置流程。
它也开始把复杂推理、科学编程和长程执行串起来。
在与北京大学数学团队合作的研究中，Hy4找到了Méndez–Pinto–Villarreal猜想的反例，进一步提出新条件完善猜想，并对相关证明进行Lean形式化验证。
这些能力现在已经可以通过WorkBuddy、CodeBuddy体验。即日起至11月15日23:59还有限时免费体验！
朋友们要是手上还有什么搁了很久、总嫌麻烦的活儿，可以趁这会儿给Hy4安排一下~
最后再提醒一波，主打极低推理成本、适合端侧与高并发Agent编排的Hy4 flash也已经在路上了。

Worker不够了主管Agent还能自己招！
文婷 发自 凹非寺
量子位 | 公众号QbitAI
一位AI主编领着三位AI小编，分别盯紧前沿大模型、开源项目和大厂人事。
我把选题需求往主编Agent Sienna手里一塞，它转头便拆起了活，派人、收稿，汇总一气呵成。
不到8分钟，它就给我端来了6条新鲜热辣的AI选题：
不er，我茶都还没泡开呢，一天的选题工作就这么哼哧哼哧地跑完了？！
早在半年前，LobeHub团队就开始用自家的AI协作平台搞研发，让Agent参与派任务、写代码，甚至排查Bug。
现在，AI已经成了LobeHub团队研发流程里的常驻成员。
在FrontierHarness的30道软件工程任务中，其优化后的Agent Harness使用Kimi K3完成了21道，通过率达70%，每道成功任务的成本中位数为1.68美元（约11.21元人民币），超过了Codex和Claude Code。
真没想到，DeepSeek最近还在探索Super-Agent架构，LobeHub早在5月份就已经把类似的人机协同思路做成了产品，甚至直接开源了！
如今，LobeHub团队已经把这套工作方式用进了日常研发，让Agent自己拆任务、派活、写代码，甚至帮忙审查修改。
GitHub上，LobeHub目前也已经一口气狂揽8.44万Star。
那么，LobeHub究竟是怎样让Agent们从单打独斗走向团队协作的？默契度如何？它究竟又能把工作推进到哪一步？
AI开发AI，LobeHub开发自己
AI给AI派活，AI给AI审代码。
这样的场景，如今早已成了LobeHub研发团队的日常。
就拿10月28日提交的一次开发任务来说。
当时，团队希望给任务工具和命令行界面补上一项新功能，让Agent能够在创建任务时，直接指定使用哪个模型。
所以，他们把这活交给了主管Agent Nasa。
接到需求后，Nasa马上创建了一个编号为T-1149的任务，并直接把活派给了对应的Coding Agent Dario。
接到任务后，Dario埋头便敲起了代码。
从实现功能、补充测试到检查运行结果，一通操作下来，它顺利交出了一份正儿八经的Pull Request，编号#21852。
△Nasa派活记录、Dario提交PR
但任务还没完。
代码刚交上去，另一位AI同事就赶来“挑刺”了。
这次出场的是OpenAI的Codex代码审查机器人。
Codex对着交上来的代码一通检查，很快便挑出了几个需要处理的问题。
Dario也没闲着，接到反馈后，它转头就去修改代码、补测试，最后再把作业交回去。
就这样，Codex和Dario就活像现实中的开发工程师和代码Reviewer一样，一个负责写，一个负责揪bug，你来我往，愣是把代码打磨了好几轮。
最终，这份PR终于顺利通过了人工审阅并合并进了LobeHub的代码库，一条真实的AI研发协作链就这么跑通了。
△Codex审查意见、Dario修改记录、PR合并状态
更有趣的是，LobeHub的Agent甚至已经不满足于单兵作战，开始主动跨项目找其他AI同事搭把手了。
比如，当Agent-foundry项目需要lobe-ui组件库增加自定义中性色支持时。
放在以前，肯定少不了两边的开发者沟通需求、协调修改，再通知对方更新。
但这次，两个项目的Agent直接自己接上了头。
一个提出需求，另一个完成修改。随着lobe-ui发布6.0.1版本，上游项目也收到了升级通知，于是顺利接上了新功能。
△跨项目Agent沟通记录、组件发布记录
妙啊，以前得靠人类在两个项目之间来回传话，现在Agent自己就把上下游打通了。
而且，LobeHub团队还真从中尝到了甜头。
据LobeHub团队一位研发成员透露，他已经整整三个月没有在本地启动过Dev Server。
按照他的个人体感，采用这套工作方式后，开发效率提升了约3-5倍。
挺不戳啊，自己造的AI，反过来帮自己开发产品，甚至还开始协调其他AI同事。
这下，LobeHub算是真的把这套工作方式用起来了，而且还同步省了不少传话损耗。
那么问题来了。
把同一套系统交给身为量子位小编的我，又会发生什么捏？
哎嘿，我真用LobeHub组了个AI编辑部！
为了验证这套AI组队干活的本事换个工作场景还灵不灵，我决定从自己最熟悉的科技编辑工作下手，亲自拉一支AI编辑团队，给它们安排两轮实战：
第一轮，让AI主编带着小编们找选题，并生成一份完整简报；
第二轮，看看刚交上来的成果，能不能直接交给下一棒继续干，生成一个动态热点网页。
来咯，上班！
实测一：让AI当一次量子位主编
首先，我在LobeHub里组建了一支迷你版量子位编辑部队伍。
选题主编Sienna负责统领大局，手下还有三位各有所长的AI小编。
Gemini 4 Argon负责盯紧大厂人事变动，看看最近又有哪位大佬跳槽了；
Claude化身开源星探，专门挖掘GitHub社区里的新鲜项目；
DeepSeek则负责前沿冲浪，寻找最近值得报道的大模型动态。
一切准备就绪，开工！！
我吩咐Sienna从人事变动、新模型发布和开源新项目三方面，分别为我找出2条值得关注的最新动态；
并特意告诉它：
我们的读者是一群常年关注AI大模型、具身智能等前沿科技动态的5G冲浪达人。
大家每天通常会花5-10分钟快速浏览行业动向，因此选题要新、准、信息密度高，能让懂行读者迅速看明白发生了什么、为什么值得关注，避免基础科普、泛泛而谈和纯宣传信息。
请每个方向挑选2条值得量子位报道的动态，共6条。每条包含候选标题、消息日期、核心新闻事实、推荐理由，以及可直接打开的一手来源链接。
任务一发出去，接下来我就没再插手。
只见Sienna有条不紊地给三位AI小编分派任务，组织大家各自开工。
我则美滋滋地端起了手边的卡美罗焦糖拿铁，准备围观。
结果咖啡还没喝上几口，不到8分钟，三位AI小编就带着新鲜出炉的选题和信源出处，陆陆续续地从四面八方赶回来向主编交差了。
更有意思的是，Sienna还真挺有点主编范儿。
收到选题后，它并没有直接照单全收，而是逐条检查质量。
碰上信源模糊、找不到一手报道链接的选题，它还会直接列出一份完整的验收清单，等我批准后就马上提醒对应的Agent“注意标准啊，重找！”。
就这样，一番忙活下来，我点开任务栏一看。
嚯！
一份包含6条最新AI动态的量子位选题简报，已经整整齐齐地交上来了：
候选标题、新闻日期、核心事实、推荐理由、信源链接一个没落。
甚至还附上了三位AI小编各自的任务回执，提醒我哪些细节还需要人工复验。
而眼瞅着简报已经交上来了，我又突然冒出个新疑惑，临时追问了负责大厂人事的Agent一嘴。
Tibo这阵子到底去哪了？咋还不发重置？
结果它居然没问我Tibo是谁，而是直接顺着之前的人事线索继续查，很快便把Tibo的调岗时间和公开动向梳理得头头是道。
甚至还顺手给我支了个节目效果翻倍的写稿思路。
把Tibo和最近跳槽到Tibo手下的Cat Wu放在一起写，效果会更好哦！
好好好，真·贴心啊～
不仅能自己派活、收稿、审核，临时加活它也能接住，甚至还会结合我的小编身份，主动出谋划策。
这AI编辑们，真有点上道了。（doge）
实测二：刚交完简报，下一棒网页已经接上了，甚至还能现场“招人”
收完选题后，我又临时给Sienna派了个新活。
这次，我希望它可以直接把刚才的选题简报做成一张能筛选、能搜索、还能跳转一手信源的AI资讯网页。
而且不许重新联网找新的，必须沿用上一轮的选题成果。
本以为Sienna会把原来的三位AI小编，统统叫回来继续干活。
结果它自己先琢磨了一番。
人事小编的专长跟网页开发八竿子打不着啊，干脆不叫它了。
找大模型和开源项目的Agent虽然有那么点相关，但用着用着多少也有些专业不对口。
临时缺人怎么办？
那就现场招！
（简直惊呆我了，我甚至是任务结束后打开侧边任务栏才发现的…）
摸索了大约10分钟，Sienna直接原地新建了两位Worker，一个叫“量子位简报网页开发”，负责网页制作；
另一个叫“量子位网页独立QA”，专门负责质量测试与验收。
而且，新来的Worker直接接上了上一轮的6条选题，分头开始完成内容整理、网页开发和QA验收。
全程不用我再重新喂一遍素材。
很快，6条资讯的结构化文案率先交付，4项检查全部通过。
随后，网页开发Worker马上敲起了代码，QA则同步挑出了两个问题。
开发Worker接到反馈，转头便果断地修改起来。
最终，一个AI资讯热点看板顺利出炉，全程耗时约30分钟。
相信我，我是真没想到啊…
Sienna居然已经可以开始根据任务需要，自己调兵遣将了。
更绝的是，它还知道什么时候该换人，以及怎样让新同事接住上一棒的成果。
而我从头到尾，除了批阅，都没再喂过一条新指令。
电脑关了，这群Agent为什么还能接着干？
看到这里，可能有小伙伴要问了。
为什么Sienna新招来的Worker，居然还能直接接住上一轮的工作？
关键就在于，LobeHub把工作目标、任务进度、交付文件和验收记录放进了一套共享工作空间里。
主管Agent可以围绕已有成果安排后续任务，接手的Worker也能够知道此前已经完成了什么、接下来需要做什么。
所以我不用再把6条选题重新喂一遍，新一轮工作就已经接上了。
那么这群Agent既能自己派活，又能临时招人，甚至跨项目接力，到底是怎么做到的呢？
答案就藏在LobeHub的一套工作机制里。
首先，Agent的工作不再被聊天框拴住了。
LobeHub把负责持续执行任务的Agent Loop、保存任务状态的Session，以及调用工具的运行环境拆开管理。
这样一来，即使用户退出对话，Agent也不必跟着停工。
只要任务运行在可持续执行的环境中，它就能在后台继续推进，并保留之前的工作进度。
LobeHub团队还曾用一项客户端数据迁移任务试水：
这群Agent一口气足足跑了2天3小时47分钟，期间拆出了60个任务，完成56次独立迁移。
两天不眠不休啊…6，AI牛马们这回是真能自己埋头干活了…
△长期Goal执行记录
光能一直干还不够，不同Agent之间还得能接上活。
为此，LobeHub把工作目标、任务进度和交付成果组织起来，让接手的Agent知道上一位同事干了什么、自己接下来该干什么。
于是就出现了前面那一幕：
我刚收完6条选题，第二轮就能拿着现成的简报做出AI热点看板网页。
当然了，活能交出去，质量可不能跟着撒手不管。
LobeHub还配备了Acceptance多模态验收能力。
Agent交作业时，除了最终成果，还会随之附上测试结果、截图、录屏等证据。
所以我们可以直接查看实际效果，发现问题就直接打回去修改，满意了再确认通过。
就像我第二轮实测中看到的，网页代码虽然交了上来，但检查项没全部通过，就还不能直接算作完成验收。
这便意味着，在LobeHub这套工作流里，尽管Agent一个个干活飞快，但人类始终牢牢掌握着最终的验收权。
△Acceptance验收机制
于是，一套既能让Agent组队干活，又能让人类掌管验收权的工作流，就这样跑通了。
从LobeChat到LobeHub，他们一步步把AI嵌进公司
其实，LobeHub也不是一夜之间就学会了让AI组队干活。
早在2023年，他们就开源了AI聊天工具LobeChat。
此后，随着Agent、工具调用、知识库等能力陆续加入，LobeHub家的AI一步步走出了聊天框。
2026年1月，LobeHub 2.0进一步引入Agent Group、Memory等功能，让多个Agent开始组队协作。
到了5月，他们又推出了CAO（首席智能体运营官）相关编排能力，连拆任务、派活、协调其他Agent这些事，也开始交给AI自己张罗。
巧的是，英雄所见略同。
这套思路恰好与最近引发热议的DeepSeek Super-Agent架构探索不谋而合。
而LobeHub早在半年前，就已将相关协作能力做成了产品，如今更是将其开源，让其他开发者也能自行部署体验。
更有意思的是，这家公司还先拿自己开刀。
自己造的Agent，反过来参与开发自家的产品，从写代码、审PR到跨项目接力，真正融入了日常研发。
眼瞅着AI同事们越来越能干，LobeHub还提出了一个更大胆的目标，Self-Driving Organizations（自驱动组织）。
按照他们提出的L1—L5分级，目前团队内部已经运行在L3阶段，部分场景正在向Agent能够自主派活、接力、验收的L4“自治业务单元”迈进。
△Self-Driving Organizations
而回头看我这次的实测，也挺有意思的。
LobeHub用LobeHub开发LobeHub；
我也真的用它开发了一支量子位AI编辑部。
两种完全不同的工作，最终都跑在了同一套协作逻辑上。
这或许就是AI Native组织下一阶段的模样。
AI负责把活干好，人负责决定往哪走。
人机各展所长，最终实现1+1＞2的效果。
Anyway，LobeHub已经把这套AI协作平台的源码放上了GitHub，感兴趣的小伙伴可以自己部署体验一下。
也欢迎大家亲自上手试试，来评论区跟我们分享，你们的AI同事又整出了什么新活呀！
（P.S. 悄咪咪地说一声，其实我写这篇文章所需要的资料，基本也都是LobeHub帮我整理的哦，嘿嘿。╮(‵▽′)╭）

11月5日，基元律动（TokenRhythm）发布Agent原生模型NeoHorse-1.5-Flash Preview。
11月5日，基元律动（TokenRhythm）发布Agent原生模型NeoHorse-1.5-Flash Preview。该模型基于Qwen3.8-Flash进行训练，总参数180B、激活参数6B，重点提升Agent任务执行与软件工程能力，目前开放限量内测。
据公司公布的对照评测，相较基座模型，新模型在Agents’ Last Exam上的整体得分提高9.23分，在Natural Language to Repository评测上的整体得分提高5.92分。其中，物理科学任务提升超过20分，开发工具与测试、Web开发、安全认证与加密等方向也有改善。
本次发布延续了NeoHorse系列对递归自我改进（RSI）的探索，基元律动将其称为这一机制的“第二圈”。9月发布NeoHorse-1后，公司将上一代模型重新放回模型池，在实际任务中收集执行反馈，再将这些经验用于后续训练，模型训练尺度也从首轮4B、9B扩展至Flash档位。
这条路径依托TokenRhythm多模型平台和开源Agent产品OpenSquilla。路由系统提供任务能力需求信号，多模型融合则让多个前沿模型处理同一任务，形成可比较的执行结果。NeoHorse与这些结果之间的差异，被用于识别能力短板、确定训练方向，并转化为学习信号。
在模型发布翌日，基元律动还更新了OpenSquilla，完善了这一执行基础。新版根据任务意图选择模型档位，继续任务时沿用原档位，重做时逐级升档；同时支持独立更新TokenRhythm和OpenRouter推荐方案，用户无需升级客户端，即可预览差异并确认应用。本期推荐配置也依据十一月模型榜单调整，使执行侧的模型选择能够跟随评测结果持续更新。
围绕RSI训练，团队提出多模型差分诊断、对抗式环境进化和群体智能在线学习三项技术，分别对应能力诊断、分布塌缩和迭代效率。其中，环境进化引擎持续生成并筛选新任务，群体智能在线学习利用模型输出与融合结果的差异进行训练，将执行框架中产生的比较信息用于后续优化。
公开演示呈现了具体任务中的差异。在表格网页案例中，基座模型生成的部分计算单元格出现公式报错，新模型则展示了公式输入、计算结果及更多交互功能。发布材料还列出了图表生成、量子物理计算和机器人装配参数求解等案例，考察模型在计算、检查和交付环节的完成情况。
NeoHorse-1.5-Flash Preview现可通过基元律动官方公众号申请内测。

加速时代的悖论：
当“你的 AI”开始对“我的 AI”说话
2026 年，人工智能正在经历一次深刻的角色跨越：从过去几年的“对话交互”，全面走向“自主交付”。
过去，AI 停留在屏幕侧边栏的对话框里，你问它答，提供的是参考建议；而今天，智能体（Agent）开始走出对话框，真正嵌入日常工作流。作为国内用户规模最大的 AI 办公提效智能体，腾讯 WorkBuddy 在经历 100 余次版本迭代后，已累计承接超过 90 亿次任务请求，带动 Token 消耗增长 50 倍以上；据第三方 AI 产品榜 8 月桌面端数据，国内 AI 办公智能体桌面端总月活已达 3316 万，其中 WorkBuddy 位列总榜第一，月活规模占该赛道三分之一以上。在企业的业务一线，蒙牛通过内部 AI 创新大赛跑出 45 个“数字员工”，将单牧场诊疗时效从 1.5 天缩短到 2 小时；上海家化在 9 大部门规模化落地 WorkBuddy，将每月 4.5–6 人天的 6000 万行物流账单对账压缩到 20 分钟以内。
单点工作流的提效，已经是不争的事实。但当我们在 AI 的加速度里一路狂奔时，一种微妙的职场异化也在悄然发生：
在不少率先普及 AI 工具的机构里，汇报材料和文档里的“AI 味”越来越浓。往往是一个人用 AI 在几分钟内生成了洋洋洒洒的万字长文，发给另一端；另一端的同事根本来不及细看，又用自己的 AI 把这篇长文浓缩成三条摘要。
当沟通演变成“你的 AI 对着我的 AI 说话”，信息的体积膨胀了数倍，人与人之间真实的思想碰撞却被稀释了。
这正是 2026 腾讯全球数字生态大会抛出的那个直击痛点的追问：一个充满“超级个体”的团队，自动就是“超级团队”了吗？
答案通常并不乐观：还不是。如果部门之间依然靠漫长的会议去对齐口径，如果同样的方案还在不同团队重复造轮子，如果关键经验依然锁在少数人脑子里——那么，个体的单兵速度越快，制造出的信息洪流就越容易转化为组织内部消化与甄别的负担。单点的效率提上去了，群体的协同却被摩擦抵消了。
当全行业都在高喊“AI Native（AI 原生）”的时候，或许我们更需要一点“People Native（以人为本）”的清醒。作为一家 AI 科技企业，腾讯始终秉持着一个清晰、有温度且直击本质的价值主张：“让人放心，把人放大。”
在今年的全球数字生态大会上，这一主张被具象化为一套以“以人为本”为轴心的「AI 原生生产力飞轮」——以 AI 原生工作流推动效率提升，以 AI 原生技术架构保障可管可控，以 AI 原生组织促进人机协同与创新涌现。在这套飞轮背后，藏着智能体时代关于“快与慢”、“机器与人”、“个体与共同体”的深层辩证法。
让人放心：
唯有底层“可管可控”，
技术才能走向组织的“规模应用”
为什么在企业进化的飞轮里，当工作流跑起来之后，必须立刻由技术架构接棒实现“高效运行、可管可控”？因为当 AI 从“陪人聊天”转向“替人办事”，人与机器的信任逻辑发生了根本改变。
在生成式 AI 刚出现的时候，人们对它的心态像是在看一个蹒跚学步的孩童——它能写诗、能画画，偶尔答非所问，用户会觉得新鲜，包容度极高。但当工作流中的任务请求以数十亿次计爆发，当智能体真正进入企业的核心业务流、开始替人改代码、核账目、发通知、跑审批时，宽容就会让位于审慎：它会不会越权看到不该看的隐私？万一它在后台跑偏了逻辑，谁来为结果兜底？
速度改变的是工作方式，但绝不能降低工程与制度的标准；稳定性、安全性与可用性，始终是数字化时代不可让渡的长期资产。没有技术架构上的“可管可控”，AI 就永远只能停留在小范围的个人尝鲜，无法迈向企业级的“规模应用”。
在人类社会中，我们之所以敢把一件事交给同伴去办，不是因为对方永远不会犯错，而是因为彼此之间有清晰的分寸、兜底的机制与透明的沟通。腾讯对底层 AI 原生技术架构（Agent Infra）的重构，如果剥开技术的外壳，在人文与治理意义上其实是在确立三重关于“放心”的制度契约：
第一，是懂分寸的权限边界——“代人跑腿，但绝不越权”。人与代理者之间最忌边界模糊。在腾讯构建的安全体系与企业微信机制中，有一条铁律：智能体可以代人执行任务，但绝不默认继承人的全部权限。它只以“你”本人的授权视野去办事——你平时看不到的文档、进不去的群，AI 同样无法触碰；而一旦涉及对外发送消息、修改核心配置等敏感动作，系统必须停下来，等待你本人在客户端完成二次确认。
第二，是能兜底的容错空间——“给探索留出余地，给失误装上围栏”。无论是人的创新还是智能体的探索，都离不开试错。许多机构之所以对规模化引入 AI 望而却步，是因为在生产系统里“错不起”。为此，底层的开源安全沙箱给每个智能体开辟了独立的“数字工位”，在计算、网络、数据与凭证上划定四道刚性围栏——“不干预它的灵活性，只管住它不可控的部分。”同时，环境状态支持随时保存与回退：哪怕智能体在尝试中走错了路，也能退回上一刻换条路径重来，将试错的代价严格锁在围栏之内。
第三，是可追溯的透明过程——“打开黑盒，让行动有迹可循”。未知最容易滋生猜忌。传统软件监控只记录一行报错日志，而智能体“答得不好”往往并不报错。通过全链路可观测平台，智能体在后台的任务执行、知识召回与工具调用轨迹被完整还原。看得见它是如何一步步做出判断的，查得清偏差究竟出在哪一环，机器才不再是令人不安的暗箱。
说到底，“让人放心”的本质，是在人机协作中建立起深层的“人机回环”——无论智能体跑得多快，在关键的决策节点上，人始终能看见、能理解、能介入。方向盘和最后的“刹车权”，永远握在人的手里。
把个体放大：
从“工具提效”到“本事放大”，
人的自主性与“三个慢下来”
当底层的护栏立住了安全感，个体便获得了从繁琐事务中抽身的自由。但随之而来的是另一个关乎自我价值的追问：如果机器写得比我快、算得比我准，人的位置究竟在哪里？
前段时间，职场舆论场上充斥着各种制造焦虑的讨论：有人担忧“中层坍塌”，有人争论到底是年轻人凭借新工具淘汰资深者，还是资深者凭借经验压制年轻人。
但在真实的产业实践中，我们看到了截然不同的答案：无论过往的经验、背景与年龄如何，真正的分水岭从来不是资历，而是谁拥有“自主性（Agency）”——谁懂得用 AI 化的思维方式去重新定义问题、调动资源。
在腾讯“以人为本”的价值坐标里，AI 从来不是为了替代人、矮化人，而是把人的角色从数据的“矿藏”与流程的“齿轮”，重新变回服务的“目的”。这正是此次大会上「人类职业进化计划」所倡导的核心主张：“本事放大，职业进化。”
在 AI 原生工作流中，这种对个体本事的放大体现为一场清晰的人机分工：WorkBuddy 承担起跨系统操作、整理纪要、核对报表等重复确定的执行工作；而人则退后一步，回归思考、创意、挑战、质疑、验收与评价。无论是人力资源、行政、法律、理财投资，还是内容创作、创意设计、高校科研与市场营销，每个职场人都可以在专属工作台上随时召唤职业领域专家，将行业 Know-how 转化为手边的能力模块，并在日常磨合中让数字助手越来越懂自己的工作习惯。
当“怎么执行”的门槛被大幅削平、当生成本身变得廉价，人的核心竞争力正在从外部知识的记忆积累，全面转向内部特质的锤炼。在 AI 加速生成一切的时代，人恰恰需要在三件事上“慢”下来：
第一，慢下来打磨“品鉴能力（Taste）”。十份方案、百行代码可以瞬间生成，但哪一份方案真正切中要害？哪一种架构真正经得起推敲？AI 抬高了日常产出的基础水位线，但工作成果的上限，始终取决于人的审美直觉、价值判断与取舍智慧。能不能做对选择、把事情真正做好，最终考验的是人的品鉴能力。
第二，慢下来“用好人脑、说好人话”。工具越是唾手可得，越要警惕思维的惰性。卸下机械排版的重担，不是为了让人交出思考权，而是为了让人不被眼花缭乱的新概念裹挟，回到第一性原理——去追问一件事到底解决了什么真问题、创造了什么真价值。去掉套话与冗余，把深度思考浓缩在最真诚、最核心的观点里。
第三，慢下来建立“高浓度的人际信任”。智能体可以替你搜集资料、生成会议纪要，但在真实的社会与商业交往中，人与人之间面对面碰撞出的化学反应、那种在复杂处境中彼此理解与共情的力量，是任何算法都无法直接生成的。技术越发达，真实的人际温度反而越珍贵。
把组织放大：
融入既有组织肌理，
在人机协同中增厚资产、激发创新涌现
当个体的本事被放大、底层的安全架构支撑起规模化应用，飞轮便咬合进入了最关键的一环：如何从单点的“AI 原生工作流”，真正演进为群体的“AI 原生组织”，走出“个人提效、组织内耗”的怪圈？
过去几年，不少企业的数字化或 AI 转型之所以半途而废，往往是因为陷入了一种推倒重来的激进幻想。但从组织社会学的视角看，任何一家正常运转的企业，都是由复杂分工、历史默契与业务惯性构成的有机体。今天还没有一套放之四海皆准的“AI 时代最优组织架构”，向 AI 原生组织的演进注定是一个漫长的过程，没有任何一家企业能够承受“先把原有的组织架构、业务流程和 IT 系统全部打烂重来”的代价。
因此，先以开放连接的“AI 原生工作流”无缝融入现有的组织体系与业务流程，不是权宜之计的妥协，而是组织进化最迫切、最客观的现实起点。在腾讯长期跟踪的数智化先锋企业里，真正跑通的机构做法高度一致：不碰组织架构，不改业务流程，不换 IT 系统——从最重复的一环切入，把智能体放进员工每天最熟悉的入口里。
这正是腾讯以 WorkBuddy 与 BuddyOne 串联办公生态的社会学逻辑：技术应当主动去顺应人的习惯与既有关系网，而不是强迫人去迁就陌生的系统。
通过 BuddyOne 构建的“统一账号、共享记忆、统一管理”新体验，以及数据平台对企业微信、第三方 IM 与 ERP、CRM、HR 等系统的连接，改变自然而然地生长在日常肌理之中：是在企业微信里，WorkBuddy 直接住进通讯录，成为聊天窗口里随时交办任务的“数字同事”；是在腾讯文档里，人与 AI 在同一篇文档上实时“人机双写”；是在腾讯会议里，会前预约与会后的录制、转写、智能纪要自然贯通；也是产品与研发人员走到教育等行业一线，坐到老师身边，一点点帮他们磨顺备课流程、打通系统接口。
当企业微信群聊里的讨论、会议里的决策、腾讯文档与腾讯乐享、网盘、ima 里的知识积累在授权范围内实现“共享记忆”，企业就再也不需要每次都把来龙去脉重新讲给 AI 听。
而当工作流真正长进组织里，“AI 原生组织”的三重深层演进便水到渠成：
一是促进人机协同，让每个岗位与行业都有专业搭档。从各岗位的托管数字助理（WMA），到医疗、营销、风控、地图、智能座舱等行业专业 Agent，人类在回路中（HITL）注入语境与审美品鉴，多个智能体在回路中（AITL）并网协作抵抗组织熵增，辅助管理者与一线人员做出更科学的决策。
二是增厚组织资产，把个人经验沉淀为共同体记忆。通过“评估—培训—竞赛—认证”的全场景服务体系，企业得以系统化地培育内部 AI 人才；在蒙牛、上海家化等通过赛训结合跑出数十个数字员工的先锋企业里，企业进一步将成熟业务逻辑沉淀为可复用技能，配合底层对个人经验的提炼、去标识与审核，把某一位先锋员工摸索出的有效工作流沉淀为整个团队可直接复用的资产——“让一个人做成的事，成为所有人的起点。”
三是激发创新涌现，形成反哺工作流的正向循环。当组织资产越积越厚、调用门槛越来越低，最懂业务的普通员工不再只是流程的执行者，而成为新工具、新工作流的创造者。组织内部的“创新涌现”又源源不断地反哺回业务工作流，推动整个飞轮循环增强，最终锻造出可交付、可验证、可持续的生产力。
以人为本，回到“人”本身
在漫长的任务链条中，微小的误差会随着步骤累积。这个简单的数学规律提醒我们：AI 越擅长处理确定性的执行，人类就越要为不确定性的方向与价值负责。
当智能体走出对话框，腾讯在 2026 全球数字生态大会上展示的这套以“以人为本”为轴心的 AI 原生生产力飞轮——用高效运行、可管可控的技术架构“让人放心”，用开放连接的工作流与人机协同的组织进化“把人放大”——最终指向的，其实是一种极其朴素的回归：
不让沟通变成机器与机器的空转，而是让交流回归人与人的真诚；不让技术成为悬在头顶的焦虑，而是让它成为托举普通人本事与创造力的底座。
机器的归机器，人类的归人类。在 AI 加速狂奔的时代，愿我们拥有随时调用智能的从容，也保有慢下来思考、品鉴与彼此信任的定力。用让人放心的技术，去迎接那个把人放大的未来。

11月6日，清华大学举行“新技术激发文化新活力，用AI讲好中国故事”鲸锐AI创作大赛大咖对谈活动
“好的作品一定要创作者去用心打磨、去主宰内容，而不可能靠AI一键生成。拼流量、赌爆款不是真正讲故事，希望大家都能做出精品。”11月6日在清华大学举行的“新技术激发文化新活力，用AI讲好中国故事”鲸锐AI创作大赛大咖对谈活动上，著名导演、编剧、监制唐季礼谈到对当下AI影视创作的看法。
本次活动由虎鲸文娱集团主办，著名导演、编剧、监制唐季礼，知名作家、自媒体人六神磊磊，清华大学新闻与传播学院副院长、经济传播与发展研究中心主任杭敏教授，虎鲸文娱集团AI剧作工坊总经理张龙，围绕AI视频创作展开了一场跨越影视、文学、学术、产业等不同视角的对谈交流。
“新技术激发文化新活力，用AI讲好中国故事”活动现场
保有初心、不博流量，作品才更有魅力
今年9月，虎鲸文娱推出AI人才孵化与培养项目“虎鲸AI人才计划”，并同步启动“鲸锐AI创作大赛”，旨在寻找最会讲故事的AI创作者，并特别邀请唐季礼担任赛事评审团首席专家。作为国内首个总奖金池达1000万元的AI视频创作大赛，鲸锐AI创作大赛共设置265个获奖名额，单项奖金最高200万元，面向个人及团队开放，不限AI创作工具、不限作品题材，作品征集将在11月22日截止。
投身电影行业四十余年的唐季礼导演，拍摄过《红番区》《警察故事3》《神话》等享誉全球的电影佳作。随着AI技术的快速发展，近两年他也成为华语电影界最积极拥抱AI的导演之一，并坚持以电影工业标准训练动作生成模型，其担任总监制的AI短剧作品《风水天师》累计播放量已经突破13亿。“每个阶段的技术改革都会改变创作方式，AI会提供很多创作工具，但观众永远关注好故事。要找到跨文化、唤起共情的故事，需要我们下更多功夫。”唐季礼表示。
图说：著名导演、编剧、监制，“鲸锐AI创作大赛”评审团首席专家唐季礼
面对AI时代的到来，作家六神磊磊选择的是另一种突破——利用AI技术，从文学创作拓展到影视创作。这位以“重读中国文学经典”为读者熟知的作家，近两年也创作出不少AI短片。当AI把影像表达的门槛降下来，那些他读了多年、也评了多年的中国经典故事，有了焕发新生机的可能。
“中国经典故事是创作的宝藏，小人物、平视感和共鸣感仍是打动观众的重要因素。经典作品的恢宏、多元及其留下的想象空间，也为AI影像创作留下了发挥空间。”六神磊磊认为，市场上对中国经典故事的AI创作改编并不少见，AI工具是先进和锐利的，怀着什么初心去使用决定了创作出的作品会是什么样子，保有人文情怀不博流量，不但是责任感，也让作品更有魅力。活动现场，他也透露自己正在准备作品参加鲸锐AI创作大赛。
图说：知名作家、自媒体人六神磊磊
AI创作不仅要有数量、更要追求精品
据DataEye研究院预计，2026年国内AI剧、漫剧市场规模将突破400亿元，用户规模超过6亿人；产量上，仅上半年单一平台新增的AI剧、漫剧就达22.19万部。而在繁荣的另一面，行业活跃承制方却从一季度的1216家降至698家。内容行业的竞争焦点，正在从“谁能制造爆款”转向“谁能持续产出精品内容”。
在杭敏看来，AI内容的精品化转型迫在眉睫，用AI讲好中国故事则成为解题的关键密码之一。这不仅是商业议题，更是文化议题。
“政策、技术和需求红利给了AI内容前所未有的发展机会，但AI内容数量的繁荣和质量的参差不齐之间依然存在明显的矛盾”，杭敏表示，AI创作不仅要有作品数量的增长，更要追求精品内容的高峰，“青年既是内容的创作者，也是中国故事的传播者，希望更多青年人才把握时代机遇，加入到AI内容创作的尝试当中去，走向国际舞台，更好地传播中国文化。”
图说：清华大学新闻与传播学院副院长、经济传播与发展研究中心主任杭敏教授
创作者加码精品内容，也需要产业的成熟机制支持。虎鲸文娱集团AI剧作工坊总经理张龙认为，AI创作是技术与艺术的融合产物。AI改变的是创作的执行方式，而不是创作的决策主体；工具的价值在于让创作者的想象准确落地，而非替代创作者的判断。要用AI讲好故事，技术应当退到创作幕后，和创作者一起定义新一代内容工业的生产标准。
张龙表示：“工具最终的目的是还原创作者的意图。”他以虎鲸文娱新近上线的行业首个AI影视制作与管理平台“鲸锐AI”为例分享了业内前沿的技术产品探索。与“一键生成”的流水线创作不同，鲸锐AI平台覆盖从剧本分镜拆解、美术资产生成、多模型组合制作到后期调色增强的完整生产链路；300余项精控能力和百人实时协作能力，更切中精品AI内容创作的实际生产需求。
“AI技术带来创作平权后，对创作团队的能力要求不降反升。”张龙说，“AI影视创作不是一个人会用模型就能做出不错的片子，创作团队的每个人在每个环节和AI精准配合，才能够完成一次优秀审美意志的集成。”

items.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
items.desc: • A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who colle
items.content:
• A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who collect training data while the robots clean — making the service cheaper than you'd expect for something this futuristic.
• Cute but clumsy — The four-and-a-half-foot robot climbed stairs like it was drunk, knocked over olive oil, and left taps dripping — but impressively reattached its toilet brush wand three times.
• The Jetsons, with caveats — If autonomous cleaning robots become real, the human cost could be steep: cleaning workers could lose their jobs, and U.S. policy is nowhere near ready to handle that.
" data-chronoton-post-id="1148090" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1">
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.
But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.
When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)
You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. items.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
items.desc: • Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansion and Se
items.content:
• Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansion and Senate seat—with candidates who campaigned hard against data centers—has the industry bracing for moratoriums and permit freezes.
• The projects at stake are enormous: Two facilities alone—Stargate Frontier and Nexus Hubbard—represent thousands of megawatts of planned AI infrastructure, making any slowdown a serious blow to Big Tech's ambitions and the broader economy.
• Voters sent a clear message: Across the US, midterm voters backed efforts to shield ratepayers from data center-driven electricity costs and supported outright bans on new facilities—a sign that Big Tech has badly failed to convince the public that AI will actually improve their lives.
• Governing is harder than campaigning: Local officials, complicated county-by-county politics, and construction unions that backed Democratic candidates could all complicate any push for a sweeping moratorium.
" data-chronoton-post-id="1148043" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1">
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.
Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.
Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.
The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.
That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.
The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.
Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.
It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.
This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.
Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

items.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
items.desc: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communication
items.content:
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT
This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.
Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

items.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
items.desc: • Rules over reasoning: Instead of trying to peer inside AI "brains" to ensure good behavior, a growing group of researchers wants to design incentive systems t
items.content:
• Rules over reasoning: Instead of trying to peer inside AI "brains" to ensure good behavior, a growing group of researchers wants to design incentive systems that make following the rules the most rational choice—regardless of what's actually happening under the hood.
• Catching AI playing dumb: One proposed trick involves rewarding models not just for test performance, but for how well their answers predict what a second model would say—making deliberate underperformance a losing strategy.
• Cops, citizens, and collusion: Princeton's Elad Hazan envisions AI models taking turns as "solvers" and "auditors," borrowing from human systems like law enforcement—though the risk of agents colluding remains a real and unsolved problem.
• The market may be the biggest obstacle: Even a perfectly aligned AI could lose out if it's slower or costlier than a less scrupulous competitor—raising the uncomfortable question of whether the real mechanism in need of a redesign is the free market itself.
" data-chronoton-post-id="1147934" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1">
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.
Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.
A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).
Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.
The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.
A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”
Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.
During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.
There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

items.content:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.
Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).
The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.
It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).
But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.
So one month in, who’s on board?
Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.
There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.
The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).
As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.
But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.
In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.
But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.
Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.
But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.
In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.
Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.
One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.
But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time

items.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics

items.content:
In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.
Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT
Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:
Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.
Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.
Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.
Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.
Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

items.content:
When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.
The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.
Measure the software that ships
A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.
Match the model to the task
Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.
Change the economics of repeated use
Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.
Test the operating model
At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.
That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.
Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.
HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.
Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.
Build for adoption, not rationing
Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.
As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.
